questiontext.text:
For each function below, decide whether it is an integral of \(f(x) = {@fx@}\).

Differentiate each function to decide.

  1. \({@cand[1]@}\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
  2. \({@cand[2]@}\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]
  3. \({@cand[3]@}\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]
  4. \({@cand[4]@}\) [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]
  5. \({@cand[5]@}\) [[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]
[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A function is an integral of \(f(x)\) exactly when its derivative is \(f(x)\). Every integral of \(f(x) = {@fx@}\) has the form \({@Fx@} + c\): adding a constant changes nothing, because a constant differentiates to \(0\).

questiondescription.text:
Integration: recognising integrals by differentiating

Grade 12 CBE Core 4.2: Decide by differentiating whether each of five functions is an integral of a given quadratic.

Core

This question is original to this project.

node.description: Rejected an integral plus a constant

truefeedback.text: \({@ty[1]@}\) and \({@ty[2]@}\) both differentiate to \(f(x)\): adding a constant changes nothing. Every integral of \(f(x)\) has the form \({@Fx@} + c\).

node.description: Took the derivative for an integral

truefeedback.text: \({@ty[3]@}\) is the derivative of \(f(x)\), not an integral: differentiating it gives \({@2*aa@}\).
Differentiate \({@ty[4]@}\): you get \({@diff(ty[4],x)@}\), not \(f(x)\). The power was raised but not divided by the new power.
Differentiate \({@ty[5]@}\): the \({@bb@}\) disappears, leaving \({@aa*x^2@}\), not \(f(x)\). The constant \({@bb@}\) integrates to \({@bb*x@}\).

falsefeedback.text: \({@ncorrect@}\) of \(5\) are right. A function is an integral of \(f(x)\) exactly when its derivative is \(f(x)\).
